html:
The Golden Bull of 1222 was a charter issued by King Andrew II of Hungary, who was forced by his nobles to grant it. It is one of the first documents in Europe to set legal limits on a king, issued seven years after England's Magna Carta.

Andrew had given away huge royal estates to favourites and raised money with new taxes, debased coins and the leasing of royal revenues. The lesser nobles and royal servants, squeezed by the great lords, rose against him. The bull, sealed with gold, promised:

  • that nobles could not be arrested or punished without trial
  • that they paid no taxes and owed no military service abroad unless paid
  • that whole counties could not be given away
  • a yearly assembly at Székesfehérvár where complaints could be heard
  • that nobles could resist the king if he broke these terms

Andrew did not keep it well, but it was renewed and became a foundation of Hungarian law. Hungarian nobles claimed its right of resistance until it was dropped in 1687.
